title: Fossils, Rocks, and Time: The Numeric Time Scale — U.S. Geological Survey
learningObjectives: Understand that the half-life is the time required for one-half of parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms
Understand how discovery of radioactivity allows numeric age dating of rocks in thousands to billions of years
Understand how isotopic measurements of parent-daughter series combined with relative ages assign numeric ages to geologic materials

explanations.text: Radioactive decay occurs at a constant rate described by half-life, the time needed for exactly half of the parent atoms to decay to stable daughter atoms.

evidence.quote: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the length of time required for exactly one-half of the parent atoms to decay to daughter atoms.
A radioactive isotope (the parent) of one chemical element naturally converts to a stable isotope (the daughter) of another chemical element

explanations.text: Minerals containing naturally occurring radioactive elements can be used to calculate numeric ages of rocks, extending dating from thousands to billions of years.

evidence.quote: The assignment of ages of rocks in thousands, millions, and billions of years was made possible by the discovery of radioactivity.

explanations.text: Numeric ages for the geologic time scale are obtained by isotopic techniques on minerals combined with relative ages from fossils, using several parent-daughter decay series.

evidence.quote: To allow us to assign numeric ages to the geologic time scale
four parent/daughter decay series are especially useful: carbon to nitrogen, potassium to argon, rubidium to strontium, and uranium to lead.
